skill.name: Connect two texts: what one adds to the other
skill.why: One text rarely tells the whole story. A second text can fill the gaps.
skill.how: Read both. Ask what Text B tells you that Text A didn't.

beats.say: Two texts about one thing can work as a team.
Text A gives you some facts.
beats.show: Text A: **The footy oval is closed today.**

beats.say: Text B adds something new. Here, it's the reason.
beats.show: Text B: The oval is closed **because a sinkhole opened up**.

beats.say: So ask: what does B tell me that A didn't?
Careful: if both texts say it, it isn't new.

encounters.frame: Wren is studying platypuses. The Bridgle is carrying facts between her book and her notes.
encounters.text: Text A (an encyclopedia entry): The platypus is a small, shy animal found in rivers and creeks in eastern Australia. It has a flat bill like a duck's, webbed feet and thick brown fur. Platypuses dive underwater to hunt for food, with their eyes, ears and nostrils shut. Instead, they find food by sensing tiny electric signals from the bodies of worms, shrimp and insect larvae. Males have a sharp spur on each back leg that can deliver a painful venom. Text B (Wren's survey notes): Spent the whole evening at Stringybark Creek. Saw two platypuses just after sunset, diving again and again near the fallen log to find food. Each dive lasted about thirty seconds. One came up chewing so hard that I could hear it. Gravel in its cheeks helps it grind up food, because adults have no teeth. Counted fifty-six dives in an hour. Did not see the sharp spurs that males have on their back legs, so they may both have been females.

encounters.text: Text A (a notice from Hollowgum Space Centre): The launch of the Kestrel 2 rocket has been delayed. It will now take off on Thursday at 6 am, three days later than planned. Kestrel 2 will carry a small weather satellite into orbit, where it will help scientists track storms over the Southern Ocean. Visitors with tickets for Monday's launch can use them on Thursday instead. Text B (an engineer's blog): Here's what really held us up. On Sunday morning, we found that a pair of seagulls had built a nest on the launch tower, right beside the rocket. There were two speckled eggs in it. We can't launch with birds that close, and moving an active nest is against the rules. So we called a wildlife expert, who said the eggs were about to hatch. We decided to wait. The chicks hatched on Tuesday, and the whole family has now moved to a quieter roof. Our weather satellite is still safe and ready to go.

encounters.text: Text A (Maxx's stream, 1 December): Vanta-fans, this is the big one. Deep in the Hollowgum bush there's a place locals call the Moaning Cave, and on windy nights you can hear ghostly wails echoing out of it for kilometres. Nobody has ever dared to film inside. Some people say the cave is cursed, but curses are no match for a guy with four million followers. Well, tonight, your boy Maxx is going in with three cameras, a floodlight and a smoke machine for extra atmosphere. If there's a ghost in there, I'll catch it live, and I'll probably catch a few rare creatures while I'm at it. Text B (a sign at the cave entrance): Moaning Cave Nature Reserve. The famous moaning sound is made by wind rushing through narrow holes in the limestone, in the same way that air makes a note when it moves across the top of a bottle. The cave is home to one of the last colonies of the endangered bent-wing bat. Between November and February, the mothers raise their pups here, and bright lights, smoke or loud noise can cause them to abandon their young. For this reason, the cave is closed to all visitors during these months. Entering without a permit is against the law and carries a heavy fine.

encounters.frame: The Bridgle is carrying facts between an old diary and a museum plaque about the same shipwreck. Help it sort them.
encounters.text: Text A (from the diary of Ada Cole, aged twelve, the lighthouse keeper's daughter, 9 June 1902): A terrible storm last night. At about two o'clock, Father woke me, shouting that a ship was on the rocks below the point. We could see her lamps swinging wildly in the dark. It was the schooner Curlew, carrying timber to the mainland. Father and two fishermen rowed out three times in the little lifeboat, and by dawn they had brought all eleven sailors safely ashore. I made tea until my arms ached. The Curlew broke apart before breakfast, and planks are still washing up along the beach. Text B (a plaque at the Hollowgum Maritime Museum): The Wreck of the Curlew. In 1902, the timber schooner Curlew struck the rocks off Hollowgum Point during a winter storm. For more than a century, nobody knew exactly where her remains lay. Then, in 2019, two local divers searching for crayfish spotted a ship's bell half buried in the sand. The bell was cleaned and found to carry the name Curlew. Divers have since mapped the wreck, which lies fourteen metres underwater and is now home to schools of fish and a large, grumpy groper.

encounters.text: Text A (from a doctor's handbook printed in 1840): For a patient suffering from fever, headache or a general weakness of the body, the application of leeches is strongly advised. The illness is caused by an excess of bad blood, which must be drawn out if the patient is to recover. Place six to twelve leeches upon the skin of the temples or chest and allow them to feed until they fall away of their own accord. Leeches may be kept alive in a jar of pond water and used again. Text B (a news story from today): Doctors at Hollowgum Hospital have used leeches to help save the finger of a fisherman who caught his hand in a winch. Surgeons sewed the finger back on, but blood began to pool in it, because the tiny veins could not yet carry it away. If the blood had stayed, the finger would have died. So the team placed medical leeches on the finger. Leech saliva contains a chemical that stops blood from clotting, which keeps it flowing while new veins grow. Doctors stressed that the old idea of draining bad blood to cure fevers was wrong, and that each leech is used only once.
encounters.prompt: How does Text B connect to Text A?
encounters.success: Both texts use leeches, but Text B shows a modern use for a different reason and rejects the old idea.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote notes on two texts about the island's most famous band. The Bridgle spotted a mistake.
encounters.text: Text A (a magazine article): The Rusty Kettles are the biggest band ever to come out of Hollowgum Island. The four members met in Year 9 and spent two years playing at school discos and footy club fundraisers before anyone outside the island had heard of them. Their big break came when a radio presenter on the mainland played their song Low Tide by accident, thinking it was a different band. Listeners flooded the station with requests, and within a month the song was on every playlist in the country. Their first album, released the following year, sold out in a single weekend. Text B (an interview with the drummer, Kez): Everyone asks about the name. The truth is, for our first year we practised in my nan's kitchen, because it was the only room big enough for the drum kit. Nan didn't mind the noise, but she insisted on making tea every half hour. Her old kettle was so rusty that it whistled out of tune, and one day it whistled right in the middle of a song, in exactly the right key. We all stopped and stared at it. Our guitarist said, well, that's our name, then. Nan still has the kettle. It sits on a shelf next to our gold record.

encounters.frame: Indi is reading a gallery label and an old letter about the same painting. The Bridgle is gliding between them.
encounters.text: Text A (a label beside the painting at the Hollowgum Gallery): Storm at Hollowgum Point, 1931, by Clara Wynn. This dramatic seascape is the gallery's most treasured work. Wynn is said to have painted it in a single night, standing on the cliffs above the point while the great storm of 1931 raged around her. The thick, rough brushstrokes capture the violence of the waves, and the tiny fishing boat in the lower corner reminds us how small we are against the power of nature. Text B (a letter from Clara Wynn to her sister, 2 August 1931): Dearest May, the doctor still won't let me leave the house, and this cough has kept me in bed for most of the winter. I missed the whole of the great storm, which was so loud that it rattled every window. Tom came by the next morning, soaked through, and told me all about it: the waves crashing over the jetty, and his own little boat nearly swamped as he raced for the harbour. I couldn't stop thinking about it. So I've propped my easel by the kitchen fire, and I'm painting the storm from his description. I've put Tom's boat in the corner, so he'll never forget how lucky he was.
encounters.prompt: How does Text B connect to Text A?
encounters.success: The label says Wynn painted from the cliffs. Her letter says she was sick in bed, working from Tom's story.

encounters.frame: A robot company has made big promises. The Bridgle found Tully's school newspaper story about the same robot.
encounters.text: Text A (a press release from Seaguard Robotics): Introducing RoboGuard, the future of beach safety! RoboGuard is a floating drone that patrols the surf, using an onboard camera to spot swimmers in trouble. Once it finds someone, it speeds to their side in seconds and drops an inflatable ring. During a two-week trial at Hollowgum Beach, RoboGuard detected every swimmer in difficulty, a perfect success rate. We believe RoboGuard will soon make beach patrols safer, cheaper and more reliable than ever. Text B (an article in the Hollowgum School newspaper, by Tully): I interviewed the lifeguards who worked alongside RoboGuard during its trial. They told me the trial happened during a fortnight of unusually calm weather, with small waves and few swimmers. Only two swimmers needed help in the whole two weeks, and RoboGuard did find them both, although a lifeguard reached one of them first. However, it also raced out to rescue a floating thong, a sleeping seal and, twice, a bobbing watermelon. Head lifeguard Jo Tama said the drone could be a useful extra pair of eyes. But she warned that rough surf, crowded beaches and bright glare would be a much harder test, and said no robot should replace a trained human.
encounters.prompt: What does Text B add to Text A?
encounters.success: The press release claims perfect success. Tully's article adds trial details that make that claim look much less impressive.
